t: Ways to Split Array Into Good Subarrays — Product of Gaps
o: Split a binary array into contiguous parts, each containing exactly one 1. In [0,1,0,0,1] the ones sit at indices 1 and 4; the cut between them may fall at any of the three positions 2, 3, or 4 (after index 1 up to and including index 4's left neighbor span), giving 3 splits — matching the sample. If there are no ones at all, no valid split exists, so the answer is 0. Between consecutive ones at positions p_i and p_{i+1}, the separating cut can go anywhere in the gap of length p_{i+1} - p_i, and cuts are independent, so the total count is the product of gap lengths.
k: Each pair of consecutive ones contributes exactly (p_{i+1} - p_i) choices for the cut between them.
Choices between different gaps are independent, so multiply.
Zero ones in the array makes the answer 0; leading/trailing zeros don't matter.

a.n: Approach 1: Collect One Positions and Multiply Gaps
a.i: Let the ones be at positions p_0 < p_1 < ... < p_{m-1}. The subarray containing p_i and p_{i+1} must be split somewhere strictly between them: there are p_{i+1} - p_i possible cut slots. All gaps multiply, giving prod(p_{i+1} - p_i) mod 1e9+7.
s: Multiply (next_one_index - current_one_index) over consecutive pairs, mod 1e9+7.
a.t: O(n) — one pass to collect positions plus one pass over them.
a.sp: O(m) for the positions list, m = number of ones.

a.n: Approach 2: Streaming Product Without Extra Array
a.i: Track the index of the previous 1 while scanning. On encountering a new 1, multiply the answer by (current - previous) and update previous. This keeps O(1) auxiliary space and handles the no-ones case by checking whether any 1 was ever seen.
s: Scan: on nums[i] == 1, if seen multiply ans by i - prev; set prev = i, seen = true.
a.t: O(n) — single scan with constant work per element.

w: Both approaches are equivalent; prefer the streaming one to demonstrate O(1) space. Verify with [0,1,0] -> 1 (single one, no gaps) and all-zeros -> 0. Common mistake: adding gap lengths instead of multiplying, or forgetting the mod at each multiplication step. Follow-up: count splits where each piece contains exactly k ones (then cuts live between blocks of k ones — same product structure).
